Planning a Backyard Putting Green in Florida

A backyard putting green in Florida ranges from a small, under-400-square-foot green at $25 to $40 per square foot to a large multi-hole green under $25, as of October 2026, built on the same permeable, washed-rock base Florida's 2026 turf rule requires for any synthetic lawn. Cup placement and a varied slope matter more to how useful the green plays than its total size does.

By the Opera Concrete & Pavers estimating team · Updated October 1, 2026

How Big Should a Backyard Putting Green Be?

A backyard putting green commonly runs anywhere from under 400 square feet, enough for a couple of cups and short chip shots, to over 2,000 square feet on a lot with room for a longer, multi-tier layout, and size is the single biggest driver of price per square foot, not the other way around. Small greens under about 400 square feet run higher per square foot, roughly $25 to $40, since labor and shaping cost about the same regardless of footprint; medium greens from 400 to 2,000 square feet run closer to $20 to $30; and larger greens over 2,000 square feet drop to roughly $15 to $25 per square foot (Angi, backyard putting greens). A single hole with its flagstick adds about $150 on top of the base turf cost (Angi, backyard putting greens). Our artificial turf cost guide breaks the full pricing picture down by size and use; this guide focuses on planning the layout itself.

What Makes Putting Green Turf Different From a Lawn Product?

A putting surface needs a short, dense, consistent pile so a ball rolls true rather than deflecting off individual blades the way it would on a taller lawn-replacement product, and it carries little or no infill on the putting surface itself so the roll stays predictable from edge to edge. The fringe and collar areas ringing the green, where chips and short approach shots land, usually step up to a slightly taller pile closer to a standard lawn turf, which both looks more natural against the surrounding yard and gives a short chip somewhere to settle rather than skidding across a surface built for putting, not landing a ball from the air.

What Does the Base Look Like, and Does Florida's Turf Rule Apply?

Yes, the same way it applies to any other synthetic lawn: Florida's 2026 turf standard requires a permeable subgrade of washed crushed rock or crushed concrete under any synthetic turf on a residential lot of an acre or less, with no in-ground irrigation allowed to water it (DEP Rule 62-308.100). What changes for a putting green specifically is how precisely that base gets screeded: a lawn panel tolerates small dips and crowns that a homeowner never notices underfoot, while a putting surface reads every low spot as a place a ball drifts toward rather than rolling across in a straight line, so the screeding pass is finished to a tighter tolerance before turf goes down. The rule also sets no new state permit for the turf itself, it establishes a material floor a local permit still has to meet, not an extra approval step on top of one.

How Many Holes and Cups Should a Backyard Green Have?

Most residential greens carry one to three cups rather than a full nine, since each additional hole adds shaping, grading and break complexity without adding much practice value past the third or fourth pin position on a footprint under a few thousand square feet. Placing cups at varied distances and on different sections of slope, rather than clustering them on the flattest part of the green, is what actually builds a useful short-game practice tool rather than a flat patch of green turf with a hole cut in it; a single gentle swale or ridge running through the green gives each cup a different read even on a small footprint.

Where Can a Putting Green Go Relative to a Pond, a Pool or a Property Line?

A backyard pond, a retention area or a canal edge brings the same water-setback rule into play that applies to any synthetic turf: the state standard requires turf to stay at least 10 feet back from a natural or constructed waterbody's water line unless a seawall or similar barrier already separates the two (DEP Rule 62-308.100). A green drawn close to a mature oak or live oak runs into the same rule's tree-root protection, which keeps synthetic turf out from under a tree's canopy edge except where a certified arborist signs off that the installation will not damage what is growing underneath. Property-line setbacks for a putting green itself are a zoning question, not a turf-rule one, and vary by jurisdiction the way any other yard improvement's setback does; our HOA approval guide is worth a read if the lot sits in a community with its own architectural review.

How Much Upkeep Does a Backyard Putting Green Need?

A synthetic green needs less upkeep than a mowed and rolled natural green, but it is not maintenance-free: a putting surface collects pollen, leaf litter and loose infill that has to be brushed and groomed on a routine basis to keep the roll consistent, running roughly $250 to $550 a year for that upkeep nationally (HomeGuide, backyard putting greens). Our turf cleaning and maintenance guide covers the brushing and debris routine that keeps a putting surface rolling true from one season to the next.

Frequently asked questions

Does a backyard putting green need a permit in Florida?

Florida's 2026 turf standard does not create a new state permit for synthetic turf; it sets a material and base floor that any local permit a jurisdiction already requires has to meet. Whether your specific lot needs a local permit for the turf work itself depends on the city or county, which is worth confirming before work starts.

How many cups should a backyard putting green have?

Most residential greens carry one to three cups rather than a full nine. Placing them at different distances and on different parts of a slope, rather than clustering them on the flattest section, builds more useful practice variety than adding a fourth or fifth hole to a small footprint.

Can a putting green go near a pool or pond?

A pond, retention area or canal brings Florida's 10-foot water-line setback into play, the same rule that applies to any synthetic turf, unless a seawall or similar barrier already separates the green from the water. A pool itself is a constructed waterbody under the same standard, so the same buffer logic applies there too.

Is putting green turf different from regular artificial lawn turf?

Yes. The putting surface itself uses a shorter, denser pile with little or no infill so a ball rolls true, while the fringe and collar areas around it step up to a taller pile closer to standard lawn turf, giving short chips somewhere to settle rather than skidding off a surface built for putting.

How much does a backyard putting green cost compared to a regular lawn?

More per square foot, since shaping breaks, grading cups and finishing the surface to a tighter tolerance all add labor that a flat lawn panel does not need. Small greens under 400 square feet run the highest per-square-foot cost, since labor costs about the same regardless of footprint size.
